title: Became, became: the Aitareya ends
hookLine: the Aitareya ends by saying its last word twice
tomorrow: before anything existed, what was the very first word?

cards: Some things get said twice at the end of a call. Love you, love you. Drive safe, drive safe.
The Aitareya Upanishad ends that way too. After prajnanam brahma, it says of the one who knows: with this knowing self, he rose up from this world, gained every wish, and became immortal.
Then the last word comes again, all by itself: became.

teach.b: The repeat works like a door pulled firmly shut: this is where the book ends. And this week walked through the whole Aitareya on the way to that door.
Food ran from every power, and no single power turned out to be the whole person. A question came twice, who is this one, and pointed past the eye to that by which it sees.
Two teachers read the answer two ways: Shankara, one without a second; Ramanuja, Brahman dwelling within the knower.

teach.h: A WINDOW, A LIST, A NEIGHBOR.
teach.b: A window opened on gods and elephants and sprouts, all held by knowing. The inside list put desire and will right beside wisdom. And yesterday the Qur'an's jugular vein stood beside the Aitareya's knowing.
Readers differ on who the he of that last line is; some hear it as anyone who knows. What's clear is where the text puts its weight. Not on a new place to go.

teach.h: THE KNOWING WAS THERE ALL WEEK.
teach.b: On the knowing that was there all week, doing the seeing.
Vedanta teachers read that deathlessness as moksha, freedom: not a prize earned somewhere else, but knowing what the self already is.

how: Students of the Aitareya read the whole Upanishad with a teacher, ending at its closing line on the one who rises with the knowing self; the great saying prajnanam brahma is then carried into reflection and meditation.

o: four endings that close each of the Vedas
four blessings said twice at a farewell
four great sayings that name the self as Brahman

games.q: a week in the Aitareya. tap the pairs.
p: no single power is the whole person
that by which the eye sees
desire and will, names of knowing

s: the Aitareya's answer to 'who am I?' is a faraway place to travel to
it puts the weight on the knowing that's already doing the seeing.
the Aitareya closes by saying its last word twice
with this knowing self he rose up, gained every wish, and became immortal; became.
all Vedanta teachers read prajnanam brahma the same way
Shankara hears one without a second; Ramanuja hears Brahman dwelling within the knower.

games.q: a friend sees a flyer: 'unlock your higher self at a weekend retreat, far from home.' by this week's Aitareya, what's the honest take?
o: a retreat can help, but the text puts the knowing here, already seeing.
right: the text says the sacred is found by traveling far away.
skip it: the text says no practice or place can ever help.
games.why: all week the Aitareya pointed to the knowing by which you see and hear right now. it doesn't send anyone far off to find it.

practice: Count on your fingers what the knowing let in today: one sound, one face, one taste, one thing you learned, one feeling, even a hard one. Fold each finger down slowly. When the hand is closed, rest with whatever knew all five.

wordCard.voice: The four mahavakyas, and the last of nine days with the first of them: prajnanam brahma, the knowing is Brahman.

orig.note: Sanskrit amrita, immortal, deathless: in the Aitareya's last sentence, just before 'became' is said twice.

carryVoice: Your line: the knowing is Brahman, said all the way to the book's last word. A full week, done.

sources.ref: Aitareya Upanishad 3.4 (with this knowing self he rose up from this world, gained all desires in that heavenly world, became immortal; the last word repeated)
Aitareya Upanishad 1.3, 3.1–3 (the week's passages: the food chase, who is this one, the names of prajnana, the world's eye, prajnanam brahma)
